title: Context windows and output limits
summary: The context window is one shared budget for input, reasoning and output. A separate cap limits output, and each API names its cap differently.
useIf: You size prompts, set a max token parameter, or hit truncation, empty answers or 400 errors.
avoidIf: You think a bigger advertised window means the model uses all of it equally well. See the long-context topic for accuracy.

explain.md: The **context window** is the most tokens a request can hold: system text, history, tool definitions, retrieved content, images, reasoning and the answer. Input and output also have **separate caps** that you cannot always use together. A model can list a 1,050,000 token window, 922,000 max input and 128,000 max output, and output counts inside the window [[r1]].

explain.title: The shared budget
explain.expr: input + reasoning + visible output <= window, and visible output + reasoning <= max output

vars.v: Everything you send, including tool definitions and images
Hidden thinking tokens on reasoning models, billed as output
Ceiling set by the model and by your `max_output_tokens` or `max_tokens`

explain.example: A request with 900,000 input tokens on a 1,050,000 window leaves at most 150,000 tokens, but the model's own output cap of 128,000 still applies. A ceiling does not reserve tokens [[r13]].

explain.md: Plan the budget in three steps. Reserve the output first (your cap plus reasoning headroom), subtract fixed overhead such as the system prompt and tool definitions, and give what remains to retrieved content and history. Count tokens on the target model, because a window is measured in that model's tokens, and re-check when the model or deployment type changes.

explain.title: Long prompts can change the price
explain.md: On the GPT-6 pages, a prompt over 272,000 input tokens costs 2x the input and cache rates and 1.5x the output rate for the whole request [[r1]]. Claude Haiku 5.5 charges more above 100,000 prompt tokens, while other 1M Claude models use standard pricing across the window [[r20]].

pitfalls.symptom: A reasoning model returns no visible text and `status: incomplete`
pitfalls.cause: Hidden reasoning used the whole `max_output_tokens` before any text was written
pitfalls.fix: Raise the cap, reserve about 25,000 tokens at first, and read `incomplete_details.reason`

pitfalls.cause: Responses defaults to `truncation: disabled`, which fails on overflow instead of trimming
pitfalls.fix: Count before sending, trim deliberately, or set `truncation` to `auto` knowing it drops content

pitfalls.symptom: 429 responses while metrics show spare quota
pitfalls.cause: The Azure TPM check counts `max_tokens` in full, so a 4,000 cap uses 4,000 tokens of limit even for a 200 token answer
pitfalls.fix: Set the cap near the real need and keep headroom for bursts

pitfalls.symptom: A 330,000 token prompt fails on a model that lists a 1M window
pitfalls.cause: The deployment type sets a lower limit, for example 300,000 on `gpt-4.1` standard
pitfalls.fix: Check the deployment limit on the platform page, not only the model card

scenarios.title: Empty answers from a reasoning model
scenarios.situation: A support tool on a reasoning model sometimes shows a blank answer. Logs show `status: incomplete`. The team capped output at 1,500 tokens to control cost.
unknowns: How many reasoning tokens does a typical request use?
scenarios.question: What do you change first?

options.name: Set `truncation` to `auto`
options.why: That setting trims input on overflow. It does not raise the output cap that was hit.
options.tradeoff: It is right when the prompt, not the output, exceeds the window.

options.name: Raise `max_output_tokens` to leave room for reasoning, then measure `reasoning_tokens` and tune
options.why: Both reasoning and visible text count against the cap, and the guidance is to reserve about 25,000 tokens first and tighten after measuring [[r3]].
options.tradeoff: Worst-case spend per request rises until you tune the cap.

options.name: Lower the reasoning effort to `low`
options.why: It shrinks hidden spend and latency, so the same cap may suffice.
options.tradeoff: Quality can drop on hard questions, so confirm with an eval.

flips.if: Evals show effort `low` is as accurate
flips.then: Lower the effort, which cuts both cost and latency.
Use a non-reasoning model and keep the small cap.

scenarios.takeaway: A cap on a reasoning model must cover thinking plus the answer.

scenarios.title: A 330,000 token document on a standard deployment
scenarios.situation: An Azure `gpt-4.1` standard deployment rejects a 330,000 token prompt. The model card says it supports about 1M tokens. The task is a cross-reference check across the whole document.
constraints: The whole document must be visible at once
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Use a model whose deployment window covers the prompt, and budget for the long-prompt price step
options.why: The standard `gpt-4.1` deployment allows 300,000 tokens, while models such as `gpt-5.4` list 1,050,000 [[r13]]. The task needs the whole document, so retrieval would lose cross references.
options.tradeoff: Requests above 272,000 input tokens cost more, and long inputs can lose accuracy deep in the text.

options.name: Trim or retrieve the document to fit under 300,000 tokens
options.why: Keeps the current model and cost.
options.tradeoff: Cross references outside the retrieved part are missed, which the task forbids.

options.name: Move to a provisioned deployment to get the full 1,047,576 window
options.why: Provisioned and batch deployments of `gpt-4.1` allow only 128,000 tokens, which is smaller.
options.tradeoff: Provisioned capacity helps with steady throughput, not with window size.

flips.if: Questions need only a few sections
flips.then: Retrieval is cheaper and often more accurate.

flips.if: The job runs once a day offline
flips.then: Use Batch or Flex pricing to offset the long-prompt cost.

scenarios.takeaway: The deployment type, not the model card, sets your window.

quiz.q: Match each API to its output cap parameter.
quiz.explain: Responses uses `max_output_tokens`. Chat Completions replaced `max_tokens` with `max_completion_tokens`, and the old name is not compatible with o-series. Anthropic requires `max_tokens`, which includes thinking tokens.

quiz.q: A Responses call with the default `truncation` returns HTTP 400 when the conversation grows. Why?
options: The output cap was too high
`truncation` defaults to `disabled`, which fails on overflow
quiz.explain: The default `disabled` fails with 400 when input exceeds the window. `auto` would trim instead. The output cap and `store` do not cause this error.

quiz.q: A request has 900,000 input tokens on a 1,050,000 token window with a 128,000 token output cap. What is the largest visible plus reasoning output the request can produce?
quiz.explain: The window leaves 150,000 tokens, but the output cap of 128,000 is lower, so 128,000 is the limit. Both limits apply and the smaller one wins.

flashcards.back: No. It is a ceiling. Reasoning tokens count against it, so a low value can leave no room for visible text.

flashcards.front: How much headroom does OpenAI advise for reasoning and output at the start?
flashcards.back: At least 25,000 tokens, then tune after measuring reasoning token use.

flashcards.front: Why can a model's listed window differ from what you get on Azure?
flashcards.back: Deployment type sets the limit. `gpt-4.1` allows 300,000 on standard and 128,000 on provisioned or batch, though the model supports 1,047,576.
